title: GPU Reservation Ops Patterns Kickoff
summary: Introductory discovery to map Calyx's inference patterns and constraints: need for reserved GPU pools with tenant isolation for PHI workloads, burst handling for spiky nightly batch jobs, and predictable scaling for model training-adjacent inference. Discussed VPC/private control plane, KMS integration, SLA expectations, and initial sizing heuristics. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share burst design doc, pricing sheet for various reservation tiers, and an initial benchmark plan; Calyx to provide token/throughput samples and MLPipeline schedules.
action_items: Alex Kim: Share tiered pricing PDF and notes on burst billing — due 2025-08-18
Priya Patel: Draft proposed benchmark plan and sample load script — due 2025-08-20
Samir Rao: Provide 2 weeks of request traces (anonymized) and peak schedule windows — due 2025-08-19
Lena Ortiz: Confirm compliance docs needed (SOC2 scope, data residency) — due 2025-08-22
next_steps: Schedule a 90-minute technical deep-dive with Calyx infra team (Priya + Marco + Redwood SEs) — target week of 2025-08-25
Exchange VPN/VPC connectivity requirements and support matrix
Run a lightweight 1-day smoke benchmark on Redwood hosted dedicated pool once traces received
Prepare draft reserved capacity contract options (3x tiers) for procurement review
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Calyx CTO), Lena Ortiz (Head of ML Ops), Marco Jensen (Infra Eng)
---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone — thanks for carving out the time. Quick intros? I'm Alex, I own the account/revenue side for Redwood inference.
[00:08] Samir (Calyx): Hi, Samir here. CTO at Calyx, running model infra and platform.
[00:12] Lena (Calyx): Lena — head of ML Ops, day to day on pipelines.
[00:15] Marco (Calyx): Marco, infra, nets and security.
[00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Priya here, I'll be your technical lead — happy to go deep on capacity and perf.
[00:22] Alex: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your expected traffic, isolation needs for PHI, how bursty the workloads are, and what a good reserved GPU design looks like. We'll also surface tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
[00:35] Samir: To start, we're evaluating a few vendors. Main ask: we have two classes of traffic — low-latency API calls powering clinician UI (sub 500ms target) and nightly bulk inference jobs that spin up thousands of requests concurrently for precomputing embeddings. The clinician stuff needs isolation for PHI, so we likely need dedicated or private.
[00:53] Priya: Got it. Can you quantify the steady-state qps and the peak bursts? Also, what models are you running? Llama variants? A mix?
[01:02] Lena: Steady-state is small — roughly 8 requests per second average across frontends, but peaks at 120 rps during morning huddles. Nightly batch: spikes to ~8k concurrent requests over a 2 hour window, but it's latency-tolerant (minutes ok). Models are a mix: one smaller 7B for UI, and a 70B embedding model for batch (we've quantized this one).
[01:26] Marco: Security-wise we need VPC peering or private link, KMS for key control, and audit logs retained for at least 2 years. SOC2 compliance is required for the vendor.
[01:36] Alex: Those are all standard asks. We support VPC-only Private and Dedicated with private networking options; our Dedicated can be provisioned in isolated GPU pools with VPC peering and KMS/HSM integrations. Regarding audit retention we offer configurable retention add-ons.
[01:47] Samir: How does your burst model work? We don't want to over-provision dedicated GPUs for nightly jobs if we can avoid it. But we do need guaranteed capacity for clinical traffic.
[01:56] Priya: Right — typical pattern we recommend is a two-pool approach: a small reserved baseline pool sized for your low-latency clinical traffic (pinned GPUs to meet 99th p50 latency SLOs) and a separate burst/overflow pool that can be either reserved or shared across customers depending on isolation constraints. Burst can be handled by our Dedicated burst lanes (reserved cross-tenant but logically isolated) or by routing overflow to a lower-cost hosted pool if PHI rules permit.
[02:18] Marco: Can that overflow be VPC-constrained? Our compliance team will ask whether PHI can leave our VPC.
[02:24] Priya: Good question — if PHI can't leave the VPC then overflow to hosted is not allowed. In that case we recommend reserving a smaller burst buffer or using scheduled batch windows where you pre-warm additional machines in your private/dedicated environment.
[02:36] Lena: Pre-warming is okay — our nightly jobs can be scheduled and we can tolerate some warm-up. Cost is the issue — pre-warming tens of GPUs for two hours nightly is expensive.
[02:46] Alex: We see that tradeoff a lot. Two levers: (1) smart warm pools where GPUs are kept idle but with reduced billing (we have burst-credits models and partial-hour billing), (2) model-level caching and async precomputation — e.g., persistent KV cache so you don't re-run token-level work. Also quantized models reduce GPU memory pressure and let you fit more replicas per card.
[03:05] Samir: When you say reduced billing for warm pools — what does that look like? A percentage of full price?
[03:11] Priya: Typically a reduced-rate idle fee — it's a function of commitment tier. For example in our 12-month reserved plan, warm pool retention is charged at ~20–30% of active runtime while in standby. But exact numbers I will put in the pricing doc.
[03:23] Marco: We also worry about cold GPU spin-up times for the 70B model. How long to rehydrate KV cache / load checkpoint / tokenizer effects?
[03:31] Priya: 70B cold start can vary by runtime and quantization — on our optimized runtime a cold load and tokenization cache build for 70B can be 40–90 seconds depending on infra. We mitigate that with persistent model shards and pre-warmed sessions when you schedule precompute. Also we support serialized checkpoint warm pools which cut that to sub-20s for common checkpoints.
[03:49] Lena: If we wanted guaranteed 500ms P99 for UI calls, what baseline GPU count would you recommend?
[03:55] Priya: For a 7B model serving at <500ms P99 with typical batching you could get away with 1–2 A10/RTX8000-equivalent cards per region if traffic is 120 rps peak and concurrency per request is low. But because you want multi-az HA and headroom for retries we'd size a baseline of 4 cards across two AZs. That's a starting heuristic; we'll validate with traces.
[04:18] Samir: Do you support tenant-level isolation on the same GPU? Our legal team prefers dedicated tenancy per customer for PHI but will accept single-tenant GPUs if possible.
[04:27] Alex: We offer both: dedicated tenancy (i.e., reserved GPU pools assigned to a single customer) and private deployment where we bring a customer-managed control plane in their VPC. For strict PHI, private deployment with on-prem or VPC-only dedicated pools is recommended.
[04:39] Marco: Networking — we'll need mutual TLS and egress controls. Any special networking limitations we should be aware of?
[04:46] Priya: We support mTLS and private link. Egress is configurable per deployment. For dedicated we can lock down egress rules and apply customer-managed egress gateways.
[04:53] [05:00] interruption / small cross talk
[05:15] Samir: On billing, can we have burst billing only apply to CPU/IO and not GPU for certain failure cases? We have internal chargeback rules.
[05:25] Alex: Billing is flexible — we can expose token-level metering and convert to cost per-token or cost per-GPU-hour. For reserved pools you get the reserved commit pricing for baseline, and burst is billed as overage at incremental rates. We can model a blended rate for your chargeback needs.
[05:40] Lena: What about autoscaling thresholds? We have jobs that ramp in 10 minutes to full peak. If autoscale waits for metrics, we might miss the window.
[05:50] Priya: Autoscale can be rule-based rather than purely reactive: you can specify schedule-based scale-ups tied to pipeline runs, or use predictive policies based on your historical traces. For fast ramps we suggest schedule-based or warm-pool triggers. Also we offer a pre-scaling API if your pipeline can call our control plane to spin up a buffer ahead of the window.
[06:12] Marco: Is there an option to set hard caps so batch jobs never steal capacity reserved for clinical traffic?
[06:18] Priya: Yes, route policies enforce hard isolation: you can pin some GPUs to a tenant and mark them non-evictable; overflow will fail or route to alternate pool. We also provide circuit-breaker fallback that returns graceful errors if the overflow path isn't available.
[06:33] Samir: For benchmarks — we want to see cost per 1M tokens and P99 latency under realistic traffic, plus impact of quantization.
[06:43] Priya: We'll do a matrix: baseline (no quant), int8 quant, and int4 where supported; measure token/sec, P50/P95/P99 and GPU utilization per card. We'll include warm vs cold start numbers.
[06:54] Alex: Okay, logistics: Priya will own benchmark plan, Alex will send pricing, Samir/Lena will provide traces. Any other constraints?
[07:02] Lena: Data residency — some datasets must remain in EU. We'll need region suggestions; do you have EU regions for Dedicated?
[07:08] Priya: Yes, we have EU-Germany and EU-Ireland regions for dedicated/private. We'll map availability to your data residency needs.
[07:15] Marco: One more technical — do you expose kernel-level tracing for perf? Our infra team uses flame graphs and GPU per-millisecond metrics.
[07:23] Priya: We expose token-level tracing, per-route latency histograms, GPU utilization, and can surface per-kernel timings where available. For dedicated customers we can enable deeper hooks.
[07:33] Samir: If we go for a three-month pilot, what minimal reservation do you recommend to get realistic numbers?
[07:39] Priya: For pilot we suggest a small dedicated baseline: 4 x A10-equivalent GPUs (multi-az split) with a 2-GPU warm buffer for scheduled nightly jobs. That gives you enough for clinical latency SLOs and a measurable burst pattern.
[07:51] Alex: Commercial note — pilot pricing is usually a short-term commit at slightly higher rates; we'll include a pilot option in the proposal.
[07:58] Marco: SLA question — what are your P99 latency SLOs and credits?
[08:03] Alex: SLA is available for Dedicated customers: we publish uptime, and for latency SLOs we offer objective-driven credits for missed targets — specifics in contract.
[08:12] Lena: Any gotchas around model version pinning and rollouts? We want safe canary rollouts for new model weights.
[08:18] Priya: We support canary traffic splits, gradual rollouts, and automatic rollback policies based on latency or quality regressions. For dedicated you can pin model versions to specific pools to avoid surprise changes.
[08:29] [08:40] small tangent about tokenizers and tokenizer mismatch causing regressions — some misheard words
[08:50] Priya: Also note: KV cache persistence across requests reduces tokens processed and cost; if your UI queries are often prefix-similar that's a big win.
[08:59] Samir: Ok, final recap?
[09:02] Alex: Recap: We'll size baseline for clinical traffic as 4 GPUs across two AZs; propose a small warm buffer for nightly batches or use dedicated burst lanes if PHI cannot leave VPC. Redwood to share pricing tiers, burst design doc, and benchmark plan. Calyx provides traces and compliance doc scope. Then technical deep-dive to follow week of 2025-08-25.
[09:27] Samir: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:30] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had a few entity errors (HSM transcribed as H-M-S; Run:ai sometimes appears as Run AI). Some timestamps approximate.
